item.title: Finite-Length Empirical Comparison of Polar, PAC, and Invertible-Extractor Secrecy Codes over the Wiretap BSC
item.description: arXiv:2604.19909v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We compare three secrecy-coding schemes for the degraded wiretap binary symmetric channel (BSC) in the finite-blocklength regime: (i) polar wiretap coset codes, (ii) PAC codes used as wiretap coset codes, and (iii) the invertible-extractor (IE) framework of Bellare--Tessaro. Our comparison is empirical and uses a common semantic-secrecy metric (distinguishing advantage). For polar coset codes, we compute Eve's polarized bit-channel capacities (via the Tal--Vardy construction) to obtain explicit finite-length upper bounds on mutual-information leakage, yielding strong secrecy bounds. For PAC coset codes, we prove that Eve's synthesized bit-channels are equivalent to those of polar codes (up to a permutation), so the same leakage bounds apply; we then convert these strong-secrecy bounds into semantic-secrecy guarantees for symmetric wiretap channels. For the IE scheme, we use the closed-form semantic-secrecy bounds already established. Finally, we report finite-length results that jointly characterize (a) semantic-secrecy guarantees against Eve and (b) frame-error-rate performance at Bob. Our simulations indicate that Polar and PAC codes exhibit comparable reliability performance under the considered finite-length settings, while PAC codes retain the same secrecy bounds as Polar codes. More broadly, our results highlight that non-universal designs of wiretap codes provide tighter secrecy guarantees than universal design based on invertible extractors.
item.dc:creator: Jaswanthi Mandalapu, Tyler Kann, Andrew Thangaraj, Matthieu R. Bloch

item.title: Quantum XYZ Stabilizer Codes
item.description: arXiv:2607.14988v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stabilizer codes are often constructed within the Calderbank--Shor--Steane (CSS) framework, where two mutually orthogonal binary classical codes define $X$ and $Z$-type stabilizer generators. While this structure is algebraically convenient, additional non-CSS constraints may help suppress low-weight logical operators and improve decoding performance in the finite-length regime. We thus introduce quantum XYZ stabilizer codes, whose parity-check matrix (PCM) is built from three pairwise orthogonal binary PCMs associated with $X$-, $Y$-, and $Z$-type stabilizer generators. A nontrivial point is that an XYZ code instance is not automatically genuinely non-CSS: the same stabilizer group may admit a CSS generating set. We characterize this collapse, obtaining algebraic and rank conditions for deciding when the $Y$-type checks are redundant and when they define genuinely non-CSS stabilizer constraints. We also derive upper and lower bounds on the quantum minimum distance, including bounds for mixed Pauli logical operators. The novel framework includes a known non-CSS topological code, namely the XYZ$^2$ hexagonal code, and yields also sparse finite-length quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) constructions from intersecting-subset and quasi-dyadic code families. Simulations under depolarizing code-capacity noise and quaternary belief propagation decoding show that the proposed XYZ qLDPC instances can outperform representative CSS qLDPC instances with similar finite-length parameters.
item.dc:creator: Alessio Baldelli, Davide Orsucci, Francisco L\'azaro, Massimo Battaglioni

item.title: On the Role of Normalization in Binary Iterative Hard Thresholding for 1-bit Compressed Sensing
item.description: arXiv:2607.15530v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Binary Iterative Hard Thresholding (BIHT) is a simple, yet effective, greedy method for recovering a sparse vector from one-bit sign measurements. In its original form, BIHT performs a ``gradient-descent'' step, followed by hard thresholding. A convergence analysis of this algorithm was left open in the introductory work of Jacques, Laska, Boufounos, and Baraniuk [IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory (2013)] and has remained unresolved for over a decade, with subsequent sharp analyses studying a normalized variant instead, that additionally projects every iterate onto the unit sphere. This paper resolves that gap and characterizes when per-iterate normalization is algorithmically necessary. In the noiseless setting, we prove a universal, sample-optimal convergence theorem for the original BIHT algorithm. Specifically, with $\widetilde O(s/\epsilon)$ measurements, a deterministic, computable finite-time iterate has directional error at most $\epsilon$, simultaneously for every $s$-sparse unit vector. This matches the optimal sample dependence achieved by normalized BIHT in prior work. Under sign corruptions, we prove a sharp separation. If at most a $\tau$ fraction of signs are flipped adversarially, then BIHT, without per-iterate normalization, still reaches the robust error floor at an early iterate with a matching $\widetilde O(s/\epsilon)$ sample complexity rate as its normalized variant. This recovery, however, is not stable. We prove a scalar lower bound showing that any nontrivial corruption pattern, even one that involves only one flipped sign together with one clean sign, forces the iterates to oscillate indefinitely. Consequently, no general last-iterate convergence theorem can hold for BIHT under sign corruptions, while its normalized surrogate provably escapes this instance.
item.dc:creator: Arya Mazumdar, Prateeti Mukherjee

item.title: The list size of random linear and LDPC codes at capacity
item.description: arXiv:2609.06570v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that for every prime power $q$ and $\rho\in(0,1-\frac1q)$ there exists $\varepsilon_0(q, \rho) > 0$ such that for all positive $\varepsilon < \varepsilon_0(q, \rho)$, a random linear code over $\mathbb{F}_q$ of rate $1-h_q(\rho)-\varepsilon$ has list size $\lfloor h_q(\rho)/\varepsilon\rfloor$ or $\lfloor h_q(\rho)/\varepsilon\rfloor+1$ with probability $1-o(1)$. Before this work, the list size was known only up to a constant factor for $q\ge3$, and for $q=2$ it was known to be either $\lfloor h_2(\rho)/\varepsilon\rfloor-1$, $\lfloor h_2(\rho)/\varepsilon\rfloor$ or $\lfloor h_2(\rho)/\varepsilon\rfloor+1$. We also show that the same two-point concentration holds for the list size of random LDPC codes. This follows from a general theorem establishing that random LDPC codes and random linear codes have the same threshold rate for distance, list decoding, list recovery from errors and any other \emph{convex} property, which answers a question of Mosheiff, Resch, Ron-Zewi, Silas and Wootters.
item.dc:creator: Shashwat Silas

item.title: Collision-Free Schedule Acquisition through Slotted ALOHA: Scaling Laws and Fluctuations
item.description: arXiv:2609.09934v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Decentralized networks can learn collision-free periodic transmission schedules, but acquisition can consume much of a finite operating horizon. We characterize acquisition in a reservation protocol for a fixed population of $n$ nodes and a period of $\Gamma_n\ge n$ slots. Initially, each node attempts independently in each slot with probability proportional to $1/n$. A success reserves a slot that the node reuses every $\Gamma_n$ slots, retaining it after collisions. Nodes use only their own acknowledgments and small local memory. An exact finite-population Markov reduction, independent of the arrangement of reserved slots, characterizes the time until every node has a distinct reservation. As $n\to\infty$, mean acquisition takes $O(n^2)$ slots when $\Gamma_n=n$ and $O(n\log n)$ slots when $\Gamma_n\sim(1+\theta)n$, for fixed $\theta>0$. With a fixed number $\Gamma_n-n$ of spare slots, the standard deviation of acquisition time has the same asymptotic order as its mean. If that number diverges while $\Gamma_n/n$ remains bounded, the ratio of standard deviation to mean tends to zero. A diverging sublinear number of spare slots yields $o(n^2)$ mean acquisition while long-run utilization, the fraction $n/\Gamma_n$ of slots with successful transmissions, tends to one. Simulations validate these laws and compare acquisition and delivered packets per slot with existing access protocols.
item.dc:creator: Pl\'inio Santini Dester

item.title: 3GPP-Compatible Long-Range Sensing for LEO-ISAC: A Window-Grid Processing Framework
item.description: arXiv:2609.30653v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper addresses long-range sensing in bistatic low-Earth-orbit integrated sensing and communication (LEO-ISAC). Conventional OFDM sensing fails in LEO-ISAC because millisecond-scale propagation delays destroy the transmitter--receiver symbol alignment and, with multiple targets, make the receive window longer than the transmitted block. We propose a window-grid (WG) processing framework that exploits the known beam-intersection swath to resolve both problems purely at the receiver, leaving the 3GPP symbol structure unmodified: the swath delay span is folded into cyclic-prefix-sized slices, each handled by one WG. With 103.2 MHz bandwidth at bistatic ranges beyond 640 km, simulations demonstrate meter-level ranging of two targets, and 1000 Monte-Carlo trials over random target--satellite geometries show that, with an ephemeris-based satellite-selection rule, every target is detected with a 90th-percentile range error of 2.4 m.
item.dc:creator: Yi Geng, Xun Fan, Chenfeng Xu, Yu Zhao

item.title: Coded Computing for Dynamic System via Cartesian Products
item.description: arXiv:2609.39373v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Coded distributed computing (CDC) mitigates the Shuffle communication bottleneck through coded multicast, but existing schemes with predetermined worker populations do not directly adapt to worker arrivals and disconnections. To address these dynamics, we propose a dynamic CDC scheme that preserves surviving workers' caches and Reduce assignments while exploiting the storage brought by arriving clusters. The model accommodates general MapReduce tasks under a placement that is partly fixed and partly new. The scheme uses Cartesian products of cluster-wise placement delivery arrays (PDAs) for file placement. A delivery-aware greedy algorithm reassigns abandoned Reduce functions, and a Communication Array allows workers with no Reduce function to serve as coded transmitters. For arbitrary feasible disconnections, the scheme's exact communication load is derived. A converse bound under one-shot communication shows that, in the absence of disconnections, the scheme lies within a factor of 2 of the lower bound under these assumptions when new clusters arrive, and within a factor of 4 otherwise.
item.dc:creator: Chenglin Li, Minquan Cheng, Youlong Wu

item.title: Optimal Universal Coding of Integers
item.description: arXiv:2610.01563v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Universal coding of integers (UCI) provides prefix codes for positive integers such that, for every nonincreasing source distribution $P$, the average codeword length under $P$ stays within $K$ times $\max\{1,H(P)\}$. For a given UCI $\mathcal{C}$, the smallest such constant $K$ is called the minimum expansion factor of $\mathcal{C}$, denoted $C_{\mathcal{C}}^{*}$. Let $C^{*}\triangleq \inf \{C_{\mathcal{C}}^{*}\}$ over all UCIs. A UCI attaining $C^{*}$, or a family of UCIs attaining $C^{*}$ in the limit, is called optimal. It is currently known that $2\le C^{*}\le 2.0386$. In this paper, we construct a family of one-point plus uniform-tail distributions and prove that, for every UCI, a distribution in this family attains the worst-case ratio; thus, the family is least favorable for the UCI problem. We further establish an inequality, called the \emph{UCI inequality}, which plays the same role for UCI as the Kraft inequality does for prefix codes: for any real number $B\ge 1$, it decides whether $B$ lies below or above $C^*$. The UCI inequality gives an equivalent definition of $C^*$. By numerical computation, we determine $C^* = 2.00012475703610197861701176297579886254\cdots$, the first $38$ decimal digits being certified. Once $C^*$ is known, we can theoretically construct the optimal UCI.
item.dc:creator: Wei Yan, Yunghsiang S. Han, Leqian Zheng

item.title: Log Density Spectrum Based Decoding of Polar Codes for Channels with Strong Phase Noise
item.description: arXiv:2610.16363v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A decoding method is proposed for polar codes under channels with strong phase noise. In contrast to traditional SC decoding, where recursions are performed on scalar soft information such as probabilities, the proposed decoding recurses over probability density functions defined on the phase-noise variable. To make the density-level recursion computationally tractable, we represent each log-density by its spectrum, and derive approximate formulas for the spectrum recursion, therefore, the proposed method is termed log-density spectrum recursion (LDSR). Numerical results are given under strong phase noise and AWGN, showing that a prominent superiority of error performance is achieved by LDSR in comparison with traditional SC and Kalman-based methods.
item.dc:creator: Yinuo Mei, Daiming Qu

item.title: The Maximum Nonlinearity of 8-variable Balanced Boolean Functions is 116
item.description: arXiv:2610.17897v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Does there exist an 8-variable balanced Boolean function with nonlinearity 118? This is a famous and long-standing open problem in Boolean functions. In this paper, we give a negative answer to this open problem, and prove that the maximum nonlinearity of balanced Boolean functions in 8 variables is 116, establishing the 8-variable instance of Dobbertin's conjectured recursion for the minimum Walsh peak of balanced functions. Equivalently, the covering radius of the Reed--Muller code RM(1,8) in 0-resilient Boolean functions is 116. We deduce the result by obtaining a quadratic form of polar rank 6, and reducing the problem to the existence of a 6-variable Boolean function with nonlinearity greater than 26 whose Hamming distance to a bent function is between 4 and 6.
item.dc:creator: Yueying Lou, Youle Xu, Qichun Wang

item.title: Logarithmic Separation between LZ77 and LZ-End and Grammar Compression
item.description: arXiv:2610.32818v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that there is a logarithmic separation between LZ77 and LZ-End, and between LZ77 and grammar compression.
item.dc:creator: Philip Bille, Inge Li G{\o}rtz, Rikke Jessen, Jingxun Li, Simon Rumle Tarnow, Renfei Zhou

item.title: Self-Referential $K$-SAT and the Finite Analogue of G\"odel's Incompleteness Theorem
item.description: arXiv:2607.01671v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study self-reference and solution independence in Boolean $K$-SAT as a finite analogue of G\"{o}del incompleteness. Independence is defined through factorial moments of the solution count. Constant-width random formulas fail this criterion due to correlations among overlapping assignments. At a covering threshold, logarithmic-width random CNFs have a Poisson solution count, with positive probabilities of unsatisfiability and unique satisfiability. Replacing a redundant clause by one falsified by the unique solution yields an unsatisfiable companion preserving the unsigned incidence graph. For every permitted local view of a good uniquely satisfiable formula, an unsatisfiable companion preserves that view. Irreducibility defeats deterministic and bounded-error evaluators using $N^c$ clause queries, for fixed $0<c<1$. It establishes a local information obstruction, not an unrestricted time lower bound. For fixed $\delta>0$, transcripts of $N^{1-\delta}$ queries leave $N-o(N)$ bits of witness entropy. On typical support graphs, expansion yields linear Resolution width, linear PC/PCR and SOS degree, and exponential proof size. Bounds hold for semantic Cutting Planes under a partition condition and for Positivstellensatz with bounded product width, uniformly over unsatisfiable support-preserving signings. Structural evidence and the limits of acceleration strategies motivate the self-referential $K$-SAT exhaustive-search hypothesis (SRK-ESH): no uniform deterministic algorithm deciding the promise family achieves a fixed proportional saving in the exponent. This dual-evidence criterion combines intrinsic hardness mechanisms with algorithmic evidence. We interpret this hypothesis as a quantitative projection of the G\"{o}del-style local--global gap. The information obstruction constrains quantum local observation and statistical learning from bounded local information.
item.dc:creator: Wen Fang, Xianxian Li, Jun Liu, Jie Luo, Yongxin Tong, Ke Xu

item.title: A Unified Complexity Framework for Quantum Property Testing
item.description: arXiv:2608.02600v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a unified framework for analyzing the complexity of quantum property testing through functionals of the form $\mathcal{L}_{\phi}(\rho) = \operatorname{tr}(\phi(d\rho))/d$, where $\rho$ is an unknown $d$-dimensional quantum state and $\phi$ is a given function. A master theorem is established that derives sample complexity lower bounds for estimating $\mathcal{L}_\phi(\rho)$ from properties of $\phi$, combining Haar-random moment encoding with moment matching and best polynomial approximation. Corresponding query complexity lower bounds follow from quantum sample-to-query lifting. The framework yields (nearly) tight bounds for a broad class of problems, including entropy estimation (von Neumann, R\'enyi, and Tsallis), closeness estimation (trace distance and Uhlmann fidelity), spectrum estimation, rank testing (operator rank, Schmidt rank, and matrix product states). In particular, combined with known upper bounds, we show that the sample complexity of von Neumann entropy estimation is \[ \Theta\!\left(\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon\log^2(d)\max\{1, \varepsilon\log^2(d)\}} + \frac{\log^2(d)}{\varepsilon^2}\right), \] and the sample complexity of spectrum estimation is \[ \Theta\!\left(\frac{d^2}{\varepsilon^2\log^2(d)\max\{1, \varepsilon^2\log^2(d)\}}\right). \] In summary, our results resolve several open problems and establish the optimality of 37 quantum algorithms since 2015, up to constant or polylogarithmic factors.
item.dc:creator: Qisheng Wang

item.title: The LQ Digital Mode Family: Protocol Architecture and Reference Specification for Weak-Signal Communications
item.description: arXiv:2609.06427v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper introduces LQ8, an open-source weak-signal digital mode for amateur radio that completes structured two-way contacts in 4 transmissions (60 s), achieving a 1.50x speedup over canonical 6-transmission exchanges (90 s) and 1.25x over 5-transmission RR73 exchanges (75 s) while preserving complete bidirectional exchange of Maidenhead grid locators, signal reports, and mutual acknowledgments. By replacing fixed-width message-type headers with variable-length prefix codes matched to physical-layer bit budgets, LQ8 packs the answering station's grid locator and measured signal report into a single 77-bit reply. In multi-station pileup operations, LQ8 confirms up to two answering stations simultaneously within a single-carrier 50.0 Hz transmission with a 0.0 dB RF power-splitting penalty, achieving a peak rate of 240 QSOs/h in continuous pileup (4x over single-carrier FT8; 480 QSOs/h dual-carrier) while retaining -21.0 dB SNR sensitivity. The protocol family also defines three extended profiles (LQ16, LQ4, and LQ2) tailored for extreme sensitivity, VHF/UHF contesting, and fast-burst channels.
item.dc:creator: Luis Quesada
